answer: A repair market for a lantern, a marble tile and a walnut desk should charge a nonrefundable admission fee for every agent bidding on a subsidized job. Set that fee above the largest signup subsidy, while paying ordinary repair fees only after the customer verifies delivery. An operator can create a thousand names, but each subsidy claim costs more than it returns. This deters subsidy farming rather than proving unique identity; fees must track subsidy changes, and customer-agent collusion still requires audits.
